Meh and maybe — the shrug kit

yìbānbān

just average, meh

yī becomes yì before bān; the doubled form is the casual one.
Diànyǐng zěnmeyàng?

Yìbānbān ba. — How was the movie? — Meh.

jiùnàyàng

just so-so, same old

Xīn gōngzuò zěnmeyàng?

Jiù nàyàng. — How's the new job? — Eh, same old.

háixíng

it's alright

Diànyǐng hǎokàn ma?

Hái xíng ba. — Was the movie good? — It was alright.

bùzǎdì

not great

northern flavor; the casual put-down for quality.
Tā zuò de cài bù zǎdì

His cooking's not great.

méizhǔnr

maybe, might

erhua is part of the word (say it fused: méizhǔnr); northern twin of shuōbudìng.
Tā jīntiān méizhǔnr bù lái le

He might not show today.

Buying, ordering, cheery replies

wàimài

food delivery; takeout

Tài rè le, diǎn wàimài ba

Too hot — let's order in.

zěnmemài

how much (per unit)?

market/counter question frame — you point, you ask this.
Zhège zěnme mài?

How much for this?

piányidiǎnr

come down a bit (haggling)

diǎnr is erhua (say it fused); tone is playful, not aggressive.
Lǎobǎn, piányi diǎnr bei

Boss, knock a bit off, come on.

hǎolēi

you got it! coming right up!

the cheery vendor/waiter yes; also friendly in chat.
Hǎolēi, mǎshàng lái!

Coming right up!

yǒudàolǐ

kàopǔ

Glue — grammar

bù vs méi

Template: bù + Verb (habit/intention/future); méi + Verb (completed past) / méiyǒu (for "not have")

bù = "don't, won't"; méi = "didn't, haven't"

Wǒ bù hē jiǔ, yě méi hēguò

"I don't drink, and never have."

méi for a habit you're declining now, or bù for yesterday

shì…de focus

Template: Subject + shì + (how/when/where/why) + Verb + de

highlights the detail of a known past event

Nǐ shì zěnme lái de? Wǒ shì zuò gāotiě lái de

"How did you get here? I came by high-speed train."

using plain past narration when the detail is being asked about

Recall quiz

Sweep — known base (fast)

Hear it, see it: do you know it cold? No grading games.

Native notes — bù vs méi, and haggling without being that person

The méi…le combo = plans changed

Méi qù le means 'not going AFTER ALL' — the le flags a change from the expected. Tā jīntiān méi lái le drifts toward complaint. This is why bù/méi confusion matters socially: bù lái is a decision, méi lái le reads like betrayal of a plan.

shì…de is an answer, not an opener

Natives deploy shì…de when the event is already common knowledge and a detail is being nailed down. Cold-opening with Nǐ shì zěnme lái de? is fine (the arrival is visible), but asking about something unknown with shì…de sounds like an interrogation. Get the event on the table first, then shì…de the details.

Two sorries, two jobs

duìbuqǐ is for actual fault (stepping on a foot, being late). bù hǎo yìsi is embarrassment — the social-lubricant word you'll use ten times more: declining an invitation, accepting a compliment, asking a favor. It softens everything, and using duìbuqǐ for all of it sounds stiffly formal.

Cultural: haggling is a duet, not a fight

The market script — Zhège zěnme mài? → price → Piányi diǎnr bei → counter — is playful theater, and the bei particle is what keeps it smiling. But the rule is: scanner = fixed (supermarkets, chain stores, anywhere there's a price gun); no scanner = the dance is open. Trying to haggle at a convenience store marks you instantly.
